newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Bull run for U.S. propane shows endurance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bull run for U.S. propane shows endurance.

text.p: The bull run in U.S. spot propane prices shows few signs of slowing down amid persistent inventory concerns and fears of cold weather ahead, traders and analysts say.
"It doesn't look like there is anything that is going to bring this market down before winter demand starts," said one Midwest-based trader.
Adding to price endurance, is anticipation of strong demand by corn growers that is expected to start as early as next week and last until early November.

Farmers use propane to dry their crop before bringing it to the market, and traders and analysts say this year's crop is particulary wet because of late planting, good rains and an early harvest in the Midwest due to freezing weather.
"Anticipation of crop drying demand is driving the Conway (Midwest) market and that's helping to raise Belvieu (Texas)," said Susan Bertsch, analyst with Bonner & Moore Associates.
Bertsch predicts that prices in the main U.S. hub of Mont Belvieu, Texas, will average about 52.00 cents in November, about 73 percent higher than the 5-year historical average.
"The market is primarily a bullish market. There is not a whole lot of downside to it," agrees Ron Gist, an analyst with Purvin and Gertz.
Gist pegs the November price average at 55.00 cents, with possible spikes -- depending on weather and crop drying -- to 60.00 cents.
"Some say we could even hit 70.00 or 80.00 cents if there is a sudden snap in cold weather," said Gist.
This year's volatility has been largely blamed on the harsh winter of 1995/1996, which depleted stocks and kept the market sensitive to most bullish headlines.

Last Wednesday, reacting to concerns over draws in heating oil, propane soared 2.25 cents a gallon to 51.75 cents. That broke the 51.60 cent record set in October, two months after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
On Friday, Belvieu spot was assessed at 51.50/51.75 cents.
"We have been running at low inventory levels for many many months now," said Bertsch, adding it has made the market sensitive to upward pressure.
As of August 31, total U.S. propane inventories were about 49.5 million barrels, 13 percent below the 5-year historical average.
Analysts Gist and Bonner predict the industry will reach 50 million to 52 million by the end of October, the beginning of the heating season demand.
Typically the industry tries to reach 60 million barrels, which is considered the market's comfort level.
Still a wild card, however, are the petrochemicals, which have been cracking propane and ethane hard all year because of strong demand in polypropylene and ethylene.
It's unlikely petchems will switch over from propane to ethane if prices rise too high, because ethane as well has low inventories -- about 29 percent below the historical average.
"It's going to be tough this winter. There no place to run and hide," said Gist.
-- New York Energy Desk + 1212-859-1631
